description: A beginner who want to explore the NASA
summary:
SkyBlink is a public web tool that turns any patch of sky into an aligned time-lapse of NASA SPHEREx infrared images. Type a star name or RA/Dec, and SkyBlink finds every SPHEREx look in the public IRSA archive. It aligns them north-up on one grid and stacks them per detector (D1–D6) with one shared brightness scale. You can then blink, subtract, view deep stacks, click any pixel for a spectrum, and overlay Gaia motions. Every view lives in the URL and can be embedded.

It meets the challenge by making motion easy to see, and goes further: it automatically marks things that moved or changed and explains any clicked dot in plain English. It also offers false colour, guided tours and GIF sharing. We checked it on Barnard's Star, WISE 0855, Epsilon Indi B, RW Aurigae and R Draconis. For example, it measures WISE 0855's motion at 8.0″ a year (published: 8.1″).

This matters because no one person can sift SPHEREx's data. SkyBlink lets anyone, without astronomy training, take part in finding movers, and it labels every automatic result a candidate, never a discovery.
details:
SkyBlink turns any patch of sky into an aligned time-lapse of NASA SPHEREx infrared images. You type a star name or RA/Dec. The backend searches the public IRSA archive for every SPHEREx look at that spot and downloads small cutouts. It cleans them, keeping bright stars intact, and reprojects them north-up and east-left onto one grid. It groups the looks into six-month survey windows and stacks them per detector (D1–D6), with one shared brightness scale so that blinking compares sky and not contrast. You can then blink, subtract, view deep stacks, click any pixel for a spectrum (labelled as a visualization), overlay Gaia motions and open an Aladin sky atlas. SkyBlink also marks things that moved or changed, always calling them candidates, and explains any clicked dot in plain English. Because nobody has to read raw files or know astronomy to see the sky change, we hope more people can take part in finding moving objects, as volunteer projects already do, and that teachers and curious visitors get a gentle way in.

We built the backend in Python with FastAPI, NumPy, Astropy and httpx, using IRSA, ESA Gaia, NED and CDS Aladin Lite for data. The frontend is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no build step, plus the Web Audio API for sound and gifenc for GIFs. It is hosted on Vercel and GitHub, tested offline with pytest, ruff, Node's test runner and Playwright, and developed on ordinary laptops with the help of Claude Code, an AI coding assistant. What makes it creative is that it explains instead of only showing: it marks movers for you, describes dots in plain words, mixes three bands into false colour, plays brightness as notes, and offers guided tours, GIF sharing and a daily puzzle.

We also weighed accessibility, honesty, kindness to public archives and ease of updating. Blinking stays under 3 flashes a second, with a calm-motion mode, keyboard use and text for every sound. We measured one brightness method, found it flagged 35% of very bright stars, and switched it off. We keep request rates low, and new data releases are one list in the config. Live builds are capped to small fields of view, larger fields are pre-built, and the Then & now comparison depends on an outside image service that was down during testing. We use only public data, with no accounts and no keys.
dataRefs: NASA SPHEREx all-sky survey images (via the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive, IRSA)
NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive: Simple Image Access (SIA) service for SPHEREx cutouts
NASA/IPAC Extragalactic Database (NED), used to look up object names
NASA WISE and AllWISE mid-infrared survey (sky atlas layer, and WISE 0855 reference)
Two Micron All Sky Survey (2MASS), a NASA/NSF near-infrared survey (sky atlas and map picker)
